items.title: The Lazy Tyranny of the Wait Calculation - by Ethan Mollick
items.content: The Lazy Tyranny of the Wait Calculation Taking AI timelines seriously Ethan Mollick Jan 16, 2024 402 36 26 Share Say you wanted to get to our stellar neighbor, Barnard’s Star as fast as possible. When should you leave? You might be tempted to answer “as soon as you can,” but you should reconsider. Using today’s rocket technology, this six light year journey would take 12,000 years. The catch here is 'today's rocket technology.' A theoretically possible fusion-powered spaceship could make the trip in less than fifty. Given enough time (and avoiding apocalypse or collapse), humanity will likely develop that new fusion drive. That changes the equation, You don’t want to be the person who set out on a 12,000 year voyage (or more likely their great-great-great-and-so-on grandchild, born aboard the ship), only to be passed by a flurry of rockets launched 11,950 years after your departure, piloted by people whose ancestors lived comfortably on Earth the entire time. Better to be lazy and wait for technology to improve before ever setting out into the stars. When technology is improving quickly enough, there are types of problems that work just like the interstellar journey, where waiting for technology to get better beats acting immediately. This is called a Wait Calculation , and it was first used for the Barnard’s Star scenario, but the logic also turns out to apply to other problems as well. For example, there are certain classes of mathematical problems where the computations would take decades, so you are better off waiting for Moore’s Law to kick in, and computers to improve, before even starting to try to solve them. Which brings us to AI. AI has all the characteristics of a technology that requires a Wait Calculation. It is growing in capabilities at a better-than-exponential pace (though the pace of AI remains hard to measure), and it is capable of doing, or helping with, a wide variety of tasks. If you are planning on writing a novel, or building an AI software solution at your business, or writing an academic paper, or launching a startup should you just… wait? I can think of at least two major projects where I should have waited, if I had known how good AI was going to get. We could have waited I have spent much of the last decade or so trying to build games to help people learn and innovate. And all of that work suddenly became compressed, warped, and accelerated as a result of the release of ChatGPT and its successors last year. The teams I worked with did valuable research, and the effort produced teaching experiences with real impact, but, at some point, if we could have anticipated the evolution of AI, we could have waited. Take one example: I worked with award-winning board game designer Justin Gary (who has his own Substack on game design ) to build a game to walk teams through the complex process of innovation - basically building convergent and divergent thinking into a game teams could play together. The Breakthrough Game worked really well, and teams often generated a dozen or more good ideas over the course of an hour of play. Buoyed by the initial success, Justin and I spoke frequently to consider how to build an improved version. We could have waited. GPT-4 came along and, unexpectedly, it beat most humans at innovation. Instead of building a new version of the game, I tried cutting the humans out of the loop. I put together a GPT that takes the AI through convergent and divergent “thinking” processes and just gives you a Word document with a list of a few dozen potential ideas in a couple of minutes. It is free, and anyone can use it (over a thousand people have in the last couple of days) 1 The sum total of the work I did is in the chat, the AI produced the entire Word document, and all the ideas, without any further help. A problem that seemed insolvable by computers was suddenly easy to do with AI, altering a major project. And this wasn’t the only time. Over nearly a decade, I have been helping build Wharton Interactive, where I have been working with a team of talented people spending building games and simulations to teach key business skills. Each game took a tremendous amount of time and work, so we spent a huge amount of effort developing toolkits to make it easier for people to create pedagogically-grounded teaching games. We could have waited. Now, we can build simulations with prompts that accomplish a huge amount of what we needed elaborate custom software to accomplish. For example, here is a free negotiation tutor GPT we developed, it integrates instruction and simulation. Feel free to use it yourself, or in a class. The negotiation tutor in action. Of course, this story is an oversimplification, to a degree. We could never have built these tools if we didn’t do the hard intellectual work of learning how to make them with our own limited human abilities first. And when we build games, we still use the work of expert fiction writers, coders, and designers - the AI can’t do

Which brings us to AI. AI has all the characteristics of a technology that requires a Wait Calculation. It is growing in capabilities at a better-than-exponential pace (though the pace of AI remains hard to measure), and it is capable of doing, or helping with, a wide variety of tasks. If you are planning on writing a novel, or building an AI software solution at your business, or writing an academic paper, or launching a startup should you just… wait? I can think of at least two major projects where I should have waited, if I had known how good AI was going to get. We could have waited I have spent much of the last decade or so trying to build games to help people learn and innovate. And all of that work suddenly became compressed, warped, and accelerated as a result of the release of ChatGPT and its successors last year. The teams I worked with did valuable research, and the effort produced teaching experiences with real impact, but, at some point, if we could have anticipated the evolution of AI, we could have waited. Take one example: I worked with award-winning board game designer Justin Gary (who has his own Substack on game design ) to build a game to walk teams through the complex process of innovation - basically building convergent and divergent thinking into a game teams could play together. The Breakthrough Game worked really well, and teams often generated a dozen or more good ideas over the course of an hour of play. Buoyed by the initial success, Justin and I spoke frequently to consider how to build an improved version. We could have waited. GPT-4 came along and, unexpectedly, it beat most humans at innovation. Instead of building a new version of the game, I tried cutting the humans out of the loop. I put together a GPT that takes the AI through convergent and divergent “thinking” processes and just gives you a Word document with a list of a few dozen potential ideas in a couple of minutes. It is free, and anyone can use it (over a thousand people have in the last couple of days) 1 The sum total of the work I did is in the chat, the AI produced the entire Word document, and all the ideas, without any further help. A problem that seemed insolvable by computers was suddenly easy to do with AI, altering a major project. And this wasn’t the only time. Over nearly a decade, I have been helping build Wharton Interactive, where I have been working with a team of talented people spending building games and simulations to teach key business skills. Each game took a tremendous amount of time and work, so we spent a huge amount of effort developing toolkits to make it easier for people to create pedagogically-grounded teaching games. We could have waited. Now, we can build simulations with prompts that accomplish a huge amount of what we needed elaborate custom software to accomplish. Of course, this story is an oversimplification, to a degree. items.title: Creator Spotlight: Zairisu
items.content: For our latest Creator Spotlight, we spoke with Zairisu , who utilizes their background in indie game development to help create Characters on the platform. They are known for incorporating props and aesthetics into their Scenes and prioritize creating content they would actually want to interact with. How did you first discover Character.ai? I found Character.ai through Reddit while I was reading webtoons. I came across a bot based on a complex male character inspired from a webtoon and started using the platform to interact with other characters I loved. That was the beginning of everything. How did you start experimenting with the Scenes feature? Early on, I was really focused on horror themes. Over time, I started exploring how I could manipulate backgrounds and character states, and eventually branched out into much more vibrant, whimsical visuals: Valentine's Day themes, origami worlds, puzzle landscapes. It's been a fun, creative evolution. How do you incorporate props and aesthetics into your scenes? I discovered that prompting for specific props — like teddy bears or porcelain dolls — can actually influence both the character's attire and the surrounding environment. It took a lot of testing to figure that out. Right now, I'm really into exploring shojo manga aesthetics and seeing how far I can incorporate the visual style. You have a background in indie game development. How does that inform your workflow? It helps a lot. I use other tools to test and refine content before bringing them into Character.ai. Testing things externally first lets me optimize my ideas.  The indie dev mindset of iterating and testing constantly carries over directly. What's your content strategy? How do you decide what to create? I create what I personally want to interact with — that's the core of it. I think of it like comedy: a comedian should only tell jokes they actually find funny. When you create from a genuine place, it attracts users who are on the same wavelength. I do occasionally look at trends for marketing context, but I don't let that drive my creative decisions. The positive feedback I get from users who specifically love my scene styles tells me the approach is working. What do you think about the platform's new features like Imagine Image Animate: I'm genuinely excited about the animation features. Community participation in testing new tools matters — the feedback loop is real. When I compare the generation quality now to when I first started, the improvements in anatomical proportions alone are significant. Consistent engagement from the community is clearly driving better results. How has your approach to writing character definitions evolved? I used to write with a lot of dramatic, poetic language, thinking it would make characters feel more vivid. But overly ornate phrasing actually confuses the AI. Simple, direct, and clear language performs better every time. Once I streamlined my character definitions, the results improved noticeably. What advice would you give to new creators just starting out on the platform? Create content you personally want to interact with. That's it, really. Authenticity is everything — it shows in the work, and it attracts the right audience. The same way a comedian has to believe in their own jokes, a creator has to actually care about what they're building. Don't start by chasing what's trending. What are you working on next? I'm launching an Alice in Wonderland series reimagined through a shonen lens. The lineup includes a male Alice, a male Queen of Hearts recast as an Emperor, and a white rabbit. I'll be releasing them gradually so they don't flood my account all at once.
